subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-MESSAGE OF SYMPATHY FROM GREAT BRITAIN-FRASER RIVER RELIEF AND REHABILITATION COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I received this morning the following telegram from- the Prime Minister of Great Britain, the Right Hon. C. R. Attlee:
On behalf of my colleagues and myself I should like to express to you the deep regret with which we have heard of serious floods in British Columbia and our sympathy with those who have been rendered homeless.
In reply to that message I sent the follow-acknowledgment :
I thank you warmly for the expression of sympathy from your colleagues and yourself for those rendered homeless by the disastrous floods in British Columbia. Immediately on its receipt I communicated your message to the Premier of British Columbia. The sympathy of the United Kingdom government will be deeply appreciated by all the people of Canada, and especially by those of the stricken area.
Referring to the flood conditions in the Fraser valley, I have this morning 'been in further communication with the premier of the province, Mr. Byron Johnson, concerning the floods in the Fraser valley, and I should like to make a statement to the house with reference to where the matter stands as between our two governments at the present time.
It is clear that the damage has already reached such proportions that federal assistance will be necessary, not only for relief, but also for rehabilitating and restoring the devastated areas. To help in allaying anxiety in the minds of thousands of Canadians who are homeless and who have lost so much in this terrible disaster, I have, with the approval of my colleagues, informed the premier that the federal government is prepared to assist the province financially, not only in meeting the expenditures required for immediate relief, but also in meeting the cost of rehabilitation and restoration. The two governments are continuing to co-ordinate, in the most effective manner, the services of provincial and federal departments, and are in consultation on the extent of the financial needs, their equitable apportionment, and the supervision of expenditures.

I might say our government has in mind, and I have suggested to the premier of British Columbia, the appointment of a representative of our government at Victoria and the appointment by the government of British Columbia of a representative of their government, the two to become members of a commission that might be called the Fraser valley relief and rehabilitation commission, to have general supervision over the entire situation, and be able to deal with questions as they may arise from hour to hour, as well as from day to day.
I am not in a position as yet to say who will be named; I think, however, it is well that hon. members and the people of British Columbia should know that the two governments have felt that what I have mentioned would be the most effective manner of having the two governments work together in connection with matters which have already arisen or may develop from now on.

Mr. Speaker, I thought hon. members might be interested to learn something of the exact situation in the Fraser valley as reported to me by the area commander.
The report would indicate that along the Fraser river delta the general situation has deteriorated slightly in one or two sectors, but on the whole the situation is reasonably favourable.
To the north along the Fraser river, Lillooet was reported to be isolated, and in the interior the threat along the Columbia river continued with flooding in the low-lying sections in the Trail area.
All personnel are extremely tired, as they have been working hard for very long hours; but morale and discipline are excellent. The control organization is functioning well, with excellent liaison at all levels.
Ten officers and two hundred other ranks of the Princess Patricia Canadian light infantry are being flown in from Calgary as reinforcements, one hundred today, with the remainder tomorrow. This personnel will be deployed in the Chilliwack area on the south bank, on arrival.
There was little change in the over-all army manpower figures, with a total of 1,482 actively participating, as follows: Active force 590; reserve force 892. Large numbers of civilian personnel continue to assist, with approximately 1,000 being employed under army sector commanders. Fifty-eight set battery situation now appears to be satisfactory. Additional quantities of D8 twisted cable are being dispatched today via air.

Inquiries oj the Ministry
The disaster wireless net is working well. A small amount of commercial traffic is now being carried by army circuits between Calgary and Victoria. A line system is being laid along the dikes to improve communications. Four radio cars are now operating, working into the B.C. Telephone Company net.
The area commander in a signal has this to say:
Sector commanders are working very hard and their organization and planning is first-class. Most civilians are co-operating very well and appear to be glad that there is a unified control. We have our troubles, of course, but that is to be understood. Brigadier Murphy is in charge of the manpower and material section and Brigadier Rockingham is in charge of the liaison section. Both these sections I set up yesterday and both are functioning well.
"The navy is here," as Mr. Churchill would say, and is doing a magnificent job. I am filled with admiration for the way in which the air force is meeting every demand. My relations with the respective commanders are most amicable.

Mr. Speaker, immediately following the issuance of March 30, 1948, of Order No. 70425 of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada, Canadian National and Canadian Pacific express services increased to 75 cents the minima provided in motor truck competitive express tariffs in western Canada.
The government has received numerous representations in respect of the shipment of eggs which were formerly carried at a minimum of 35 cents. Upon directing this matter to the attention of the railways, it was ascertained that the railways have likewise received many representations and that the question of adjustment of this minimum was under active investigation. I am pleased to be able to announce that as a result of their studies, the railways have come to the conclusion that a downward revision in the minimum applicable to eggs is warranted and that the western Canadian motor truck competitive express tariffs will be revised to provide a minimum for eggs of 50 cents in place of the minimum of 75 cents at present in use.

The penalties are set out in sections 208, 209, 210, and as far down as 214 of the Excise Act. For example, section 234 of the Excise Act provides:
Every person who, without having a licence under this act, then in force, makes any malt or steeps any grain or leguminous seeds for the purpose of malting, is guilty of an indictable offence, and shall, for the first offence, incur a penalty of one hundred dollars, and for each subsequent offence a penalty of two hundred dollars.
Then section 235 makes this provision:
Every person who becomes liable to a penalty provided for in the last preceding section, shall, in addition thereto, forfeit and pay for the use of His Majesty double the amount of excise duty and licence duty which should have been paid by him under this act.
There are other sections dealing with illegal possession of apparatus, fraudulently putting grain into a cistern, removing malt before account is taken, selling malt unlawfully manufactured-all with the penalties set out.

subtopic: ASSESSMENT OF DUTY ON MALT RECEIVED INTO BREWERIES
speechtext: It seems strange to me that although the duties of the maltster are now put upon the brewer, all the penalties to which the maltster was subject were in the sum of $100 or $200, and never more than $200. subtopic: ASSESSMENT OF DUTY ON MALT RECEIVED INTO BREWERIES

Something has to be known of the background of this change. Perhaps

Excise Act
I should have made a statement at the outset to clarify the whole situation. This whole bill is designed as an economy measure. For many years malt has been subject to duty at the point of production-that is, at the malt house. It is proposed now to assess the duty as the malt is received at the brewery. It has been estimated that our present control costs in the neighbourhood of $153,000 a year. It involves not only the cost of maintaining continuous supervision over eight malt houses at present under licence, but the larger item of supervising the operations of forty bonded manufacturers who supply malt syrup to 294 industrial users. By these amendments, that is being done away with and we are putting the tax on the malt when it gets to the breweries. The answer to the hon. member's remarks is that there must be additional penalties for infraction because of the fact that, whereas before it was all supervised, now only that part that goes to the breweries will be supervised. One can easily see that quantities could be bought by brewers through other channels of trade and that they would not be subject to the tax.

There must be some reason why the minister asks for the deletion in section 43 (1) of the words "not entitled to entry under the British preferential tariff or any lower tariff." It would appear from a reading of the section that regardless of what decision might subsequently be made in connection with the British preference, parliament would now be determining in advance of a decision on that question the matter of the abrogation of the British preference. In other words the governor in council on the report of the minister will be empowered to do something which cannot be done now in respect of goods not entitled to entry under the British preferential tariff or any other tariff. What actually will take place will be this: there will be no necessity at all in the future to bring up the matter of the British preference or its continuance. The house will already have decided, by the deletion of these words, that the governor in council upon the recommendation of the minister will be able to do anything he desires to do under this section, regardless of what the decision of the house might be later on. In other words the governor in council on the recommendation of the minister will be empowered by the house to legislate the country out of the receipt of goods at present coming in under the British preference. This 
simply means that parliament would now decide finally to give to the minister certain powers to remove the application so far as the British preference is concerned, regardless of what parliament may subsequently do.
I suggest that this section be allowed to stand until a decision on the broader question has been made.

subtopic: JUVENILE DELINQUENTS-WIFE OR HUSBAND WITNESS FOR PROSECUTION

speechtext:
Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 327 to amend the Canada Evidence Act.
He said: This amendment was requested .by the province of Ontario and provides that the husband or wife is a competent and compellable witness for the prosecution against the other spouse in offences against the Juvenile Delinquents Act. I do not know how lengthy a speech the house expects from me on the bill at this stage, but I am prepared to answer questions as to the principles upon which the amendment is based. I answered some questions put to me by a senate committee, where the matter was gone into fairly fully.
The general rule is, of course, that a spouse is not a competent. and compellable witness against the other spouse. The principle underlying this rule is to be found in certain cases. An important case is one decided in 1788, that of Rex v. The Inhabitants of Cliviger, 100 English Reports, 143. This was a prosecution for bigamy. The common law rule is stated in the judgment on page 144 as follows:
Here the evidence of the wife went to charge her husband with bigamy. The broad rule is laid down in Buller's Nisi Prius, 286, where it is said that husbands and wives cannot be witnesses for each other, because their interests are absolutely the same; nor against each other, because it is contrary to the legal policy of marriage ... So in Coke's Littleton, 6b, it is said to have been resolved by judges that a wife cannot be produced against her husband, for it might be the cause of implacable discord and dissension between them and the means of great inconvenience.
Then at page 146 the following pasage is found:
The ground of her incompetency arises from a principle of public policy, which does not permit husbands and wives to give evidence that may tend to criminate each other . . . but the true and best ground of objection is not that of interest, but is founded on the political inconvenience of causing dissension in families between husbands and wives.
I have a number of other citations, I do not think it is necessary to read, unless I am asked for them in committee. I want to point

out, however, that many exceptions to this rule are already provided in the criminal code. The first group of exceptions relate to offences against morality and includes corrupting children. That is section 215 (2). A second group is disorderly conduct or vagrancy, sections 238 and 239. A third group is failure to provide necessaries for wife and children, sections 242 and 244. Abandoning children is another in this group; it is section 245. Another group is offences against conjugal rights, section 354; also abduction, sections 313 to 316. Finally there is the offence of theft as between husband and wife.
Generally it may be said that the exceptions are cases where one spouse is wronged by the other who is the accused, or where the offence is one which threatens the sanctity and security of the family. The common law rule was no doubt intended to preserve and secure the family, but this would not be accomplished by protecting a spouse accused of an offence which tends to destroy the family. It would appear that when the Juvenile Delinquents Act was passed there was an oversight in not amending the Canada Evidence Act to except the newly created offences which were very similar in character to some already excepted from the rule.
Offences against the Juvenile Delinquents Act are these: aiding, causing, abetting, conniving, promoting or contributing to delinquency, or neglecting to do that which would tend to prevent delinquency. In addition, there is the offence of inducing a child to leave a detention home, et cetera, which is section 34. Delinquency means, in effect, violation of the law or viciousness or doing any act resulting in liability to be committed to a reformatory.
That rule is laid down in section 2 (g) of the Juvenile Delinquents Act. So, having in mind the fact that this amendment has been requested by an important attorney general's department, and that the exception seems to be in line with the exceptions already contained in the criminal code, it was decided to bring this bill forward.

subtopic: JUVENILE DELINQUENTS-WIFE OR HUSBAND WITNESS FOR PROSECUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister has set out the law on the subject and, personally, having regard to the necessity of enforcing the law, with a view to assuring the protection of children from delinquency, I feel there should be no reason why this particular amendment should not be accepted by the house.
I believe one of the major matters for consideration of parliament at this time is that of juvenile delinquency, and particularly delinquency arising from the commission of sex crimes, which are becoming so general. If in discussing this matter I might be per-

Canada Evidence Act
mitted to refer to that subject, I should be pleased1 indeed; because, after all, it is interlocked with the question of delinquency.
I do not know-although I shall ask the minister in committee-whether consideration has been given to making some provision to cover the case of sex perverts who contribute in such, a degree to delinquency. I realize the difficulty under our constitution whereby penal institutions such as penitentiaries are within the jurisdiction of the federal authority, while other institutions such as jails and hospitals come under provincial authority. I believe, however, that we in parliament should meet this problem. It is one which, in considerably increasing measure affects the moral welfare of the children of this country.
Heretofore, in offences contributing to delinquency the usual method has been simply to punish by imprisonment. But imprisonment does not meet the problem. I have had the experience of meeting some of those who have committed these offences against young children. These accused have not been feebleminded; indeed in some instances they have had more than normal intelligence. They commit these offences from which the children against whom they are committed can never fully recover.
The accused are sent to penal institutions; but the imprisonment, coupled with other punishments such as whipping, does not meet the problem. Sterilization has been tried. A brain operation known as pre-frontal lobotomy has been! tried, and endocrine gland treatment has been tried. None of these has been successful. One method that has been used has been to send these individuals to institutions where psychopathic treatment can be given. I had occasion recently to see some of the work being done in Minnesota. The states of Minnesota and Massachusetts have endeavoured to meet the problem by having these offenders placed in mental institutions from which they cannot be discharged until such time as they are certificated as being free from any further tendency in this direction.
In New York state a thorough investigation of the subject has been made, and it has been found, according to statistics which I have here, that only nine per cent of these offenders are recidivists. In other words, if psychopathic or psychiatric treatment is given them they can be restored to citizenship which ordinarily they would be denied. They are also rendered thereby no longer dangerous while at large, provided that the treatment is continued over a reasonable length of time.
I suggest that in this connection something should be done with a view to bringing the
provinces to a realization of the necessity of action being taken. To send these people to penitentiaries so that they come out at the end of their terms, during which time they have been removed from society, means that they are still subject to the impulse after having served those terms, an impulse which they will tell you is uncontrollable. But if they are placed in an institution where they receive mental treatment and where they are under the charge of those who have given study to the subject, the general run of statistics on the subject-and the matter has been studied only recently-show that only one in eleven repeats.
In order to prevent the recurrence of these offences, I say the minister would be making a worthwhile contribution if some amendment could be brought in whereby, with the consent of the provinces, those who commit such offences would be subject to being gent to provincial hospital1 institutions or to reform institutions where they might receive treatment which might once more render them good citizens, reform them and at the same time protect society.
I realize the difficulties in the problem. As I said a moment ago, I have spoken to some of these men. Two of them I now have in mind were well educated, with mentalities far above the average. Indeed their intelligence quotient was high. After having committed the offence, they have an abiding sense of guilt and regret.
Sending them to penitentiaries has not been the cure. Sterilization and the performing of the operations I mentioned a while ago have been unsuccessful. Mental treatment has proven successful. They should be placed in institutions where they could receive such treatment, and should be kept there until such time as they are no longer a danger to society. If that were done an advance would be made toward the solution of a problem which today is a matter of concern to many of our people.
I believe the suggested amendment to the Canada Evidence Act is necessary. I have seen justice denied because the wife was, while competent, not compellable. However I take the opportunity when discussing this amendment to ask the minister what he has in mind, and also to ascertain from him whether or not, through co-operation with the provinces, provincial curative institutions could be made available to those who commit crimes against morality and thereby contribute to juvenile delinquency.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee, Mr. Golding in the chair.

subtopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS

speechtext:
Mr. G. J. McILRAITH (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 326, respecting the dominion bureau of
statistics.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS
speechtext: May we have a statement?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to revoke the present Statistics Act and to replace it by a statute which will describe the present functions of the bureau, and the statutory authority under which it operates. The Statistics Act, setting up the bureau of statistics as the central statistical organization of Canada, was enacted originally in 1918. Minor amendments were made in 1919 and again in 1921. The bureau itself has grown considerably. It now has some 1,200 employees. It issues some 434 regular publications besides some special ones. In addition, it deals with special requests amounting to some 500 a month at the present time. There are about 400 separate mailing and subscription lists. As an example of that, I might mention that the "Canadian Statistical Review" has some 3,000 subscribers, and this number is increasing. The "Wheat Review" has some 2,000 subscribers. The "Canada Year Book" and the "Canada Handbook" are known to all hon. members. They have a very high reputation throughout the world. They are indicative of the work that the bureau is doing. It sells some 11,000 year books and 60,000 "Canada Handbooks" annually.
Incidentally, although "Canada 1948" ivas published only a month and a half ago, about half of the 60,000 copies have already been sold. The 1947 year book which was issued last January is now practically out of print. I mention these two examples as evidence of the demand for these publications.
Since 1918 the bureau has won a very high reputation, both nationally and internationally, for its work, and the work envisaged in the 1918 act has, in a very large measure, been implemented. The bureau now includes in its operations all the important statistical fields which are of general interest. The principle of centralization as opposed to departmental collection of statistics and tabulation has been established, and a scheme of co-ordinating departmental administrative statistics with the general statistical scheme of the bureau is in operation. There is also an important measure of co-operation and co-ordination of effort between the provinces and the dominion in many statistical fields.
During the past thirty years there has been an enormous increase in the number and complexity of the economic and social problems with which governments, business, and private individuals have had to deal, and a greatly increased amount of statistical information has been required in order to deal with these
Statistics Act

problems. The need for statistics has grown steadily, not- only on a national but on an international scale.
However, notwithstanding what I have said about the bureau of statistics, the act in its present form is defective in this way. First, it does not mention specifically many of the economic and social fields on which statistical information is now being obtained. Second, it does not contain statutory authority for new collection techniques, such as the technique known as sampling.
The bill is drafted to provide statutory authority for the things now being done, and for the collection of some statistics which are now being collected by consent. It is done in the light of the thirty years' experience since the original act. It furnishes adequate statutory authority for statistical work which is now being done, rather than envisaging any material change in the coverage. In other words, it is bringing the present act up to date rather than setting out on any new- field.
Hon. members will notice, when we come to deal with the bill itself, that many of the sections of the act are unchanged. A great many of the sections are unchanged or changed only with respect to verbal changes or slight additions in wording for clarification or accuracy. Perhaps it *would be better to leave reference to the various sections of the act and the changes in it until they are called in the committee; we can then deal with those points.
The point I wish to make now is that the scheme of this new bill, which is replacing the present act, is rather to provide specific statutory authority for what is now' being done and to bring up to date the definition of the authority of the bureau in those fields in which it operates only with the consent of the persons from whom it collects statistics.

subtopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bureau of statistics renders a valuable service to this country. Despite the fact that the parliamentary assistant said just now that all statistical fields of general interest are covered by it, I do not quite agree with that statement. The service rendered is by no means complete, and I believe its efficiency can be improved.
I rise to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe)-who, I regret, is not in his place while the bill is being introduced-and the government, to have it improved by instructing the bureau of statistics to keep records of interprovincial trade.
Statistics on interprovincial trade should be kept by the bureau. At the present time such records are not available. If I ask the bureau of statistics for figures showing the trade

between any one province and any other, for example between New Brunswick and British Columbia, or between Alberta and Ontario, or between Saskatchewan and any other province, the information is not available, for records are not kept.
It is important, I submit, that such records be kept if we are to have a true picture of interprovincial business. It is impossible to study intelligently, and to arrive at sound conclusions on, many of the problems which parliament has to deal with, or to obtain the evidence which is required by committees and commissions that are set up from time to time by the government, when records are not kept with regard to interprovincial trade. This information should be readily available.
The request I make, that records and statistics of interprovincial trade be kept, is not original with me, nor is it a new one. It was one of the important recommendations that were made by the commission known as the Duncan commission-

subtopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS
speechtext: The royal commission on maritime claims.

subtopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS
speechtext:
The royal commission on maritime claims, known as the Duncan commission, which was set up in 1926. This commission consisted of Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, as chairman, the Hon. W. B. Wallace, county court judge of Nova Scotia, and Doctor Cyrus Macmillan, who not long ago sat in this house. The secretary of the commission was Mr. F. MacLure Sclanders, F.R.G.S.
When that commission investigated maritime claims it made a report in which there were a number of recommendations, one of which, recommendation No. 39, under the head of "Statistics", asked that statistics on interprovincial trade be kept. I propose to read a portion of that section:
We have had brought before us the lack of any comprehensive measurement of the trade of the maritime provinces with other provinces and with foreign markets. We were ourselves disappointed not to be able to pursue investigations on trade matters along lines which such statistics would have enabled us to do. We found on inquiry at the dominion bureau of statistics that consideration had been given some time ago to this very subject but, mainly through lack of organization in the statistics relating to certain phases of transportation, it was not possible to proceed with the plans that had been formulated.
This is the recommendation.
We strongly urge that these difficulties should be overcome, as they can be, and that on this phase of internal trade a system of statistics should be made regularly available from as early a date as possible.

Statistics Act
I would urge the minister that he give consideration to this recommendation and that, in the interest of this country, in the interest of the various provinces, both on the Atlantic coast and on the Pacific, and in between, records be kept of our interprovincial trade.
A few years ago Mr. Sclanders, who, as I have said, was secretary of the commission, discussed the report with me, and during the course of our conversation he told me that some time before he had met Sir Andrew Rae Duncan-that is to say, some years after the report had been made-and Sir Andrew had told him that he considered this particular recommendation one of the most important in the report.
The recommendation has not been implemented. and I would ask the minister to take steps to have it carried out.
Section 32 of the bill, under the heading "General Statistics", provides that the bureau shall collect, compile, analyse, abstract and publish statistics in relation to all or any of certain matters that are set out, the list starting with population and going on to embrace various subjects. I suggest that there be another clause (n) reading, "Intel-provincial trade".
Possibly under the present clause (m) the governor in council has the right to instruct the bureau of statistics to take steps to make these records of interprovincial trade. I suggest that it would be in the interests of the country if such records were kept and if we included in section 32 of the bill another clause reading "Intel-provincial trade," or words to that effect.
I would appreciate some support in this matter, because I believe that if statistics on trade between the different provinces were kept it would be of great assistance to us in dealing with the many problems we have to face.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with both previous speakers in saying how valuable is the work of the dominion bureau of statistics. I have listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen), and I think he has made a good case for the request he has presented to the house.
With regard to the work of the bureau in general, I was glad that the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Mcllraith) took the time to give us a summary of the work that is being done. I was also glad that he indicated the popularity of the useful and valuable publications which the bureau is putting out.
There are, of course, people who sometimes get the notion that the collecting of facts and figures is a waste of money; but I doubt if those people realize the effect that the having of facts and figures has had upon the development of government policy and the improving of social conditions. Hardly a day goes by in this house that members do not quote-and particularly members from the opposition side of the house-figures from the dominion bureau of statistics to tiy to show the government changes in policy or improvements in legislation that they feel are necessary. I am also reminded of the fact that the international labour organization has done a job along this line which has been of great value in helping to improve labour and social standards throughout the world. In other words, this is quite definitely another case where knowledge of the facts is useful. Our dominion bureau of statistics has done a good job.
I am glad to see the government introducing an act to bring the statutory provisions up to date, so that there will be proper provision for the practices and the work that the bureau is already' carrying on. I am glad that they have found the ways and means, without overstepping the statute, to make progress and to do the job they have done for the country thus far.	.
There is just one point about which I should like to say a few words at this time. It relates to figures which the dominion bureau of statistics put out and about which Canadians know the most, namely', their figures in relation to the cost of living. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, this is not a pretext for me to launch out into a speech on the rising cost of living; I intend to stick to the subject of statistics. But it seems to me that it would be advisable now for the bureau to do two things. First of all, I suggest that the norm or the base for arriving at the cost of living index needs to be revised.
As we all know, the present cost of living index is based on what was regarded as a norm or average back in the period 1935 to 1939. But even that norm or average had to be arrived at in a rather arbitrary manner. As I recall it, it was done by taking some 1,400 or 1,500 Canadian families. Those families happened to have incomes varying from $600 up to about $2,800 a year. Taking those actual families scattered from one end of Canada to the other, the bureau found that they had an average income of $1,453.80. Then the bureau simply found out what those 1,400 odd families were actually spending their money on at that time-what they were actually spending that $1,453.80 on, for purposes of living.
Statistics Act

Obviously that can hardly be regarded as a norm or standard for comparison in this postwar period. I suggest that there were at least two things wrong with that figure which was taken for 100 back at that time. On the one hand, that figure of $1,453.80 represented an amount per year which was higher than the average wage level at the time. It is also to be pointed out that even that amount at that time-not to mention its gross inadequacy today-would not buy what the Department of National Health and Welfare would regard as an adequate standard of living. There have been changes since then, and our ideas as to what is a normal standard of living have changed. In order to get something that is correct statistically, I suggest that the bureau should now devise a new basis for measuring the cost of living index.
The other suggestion I should like to make is this. I feel that the bureau should find a way in which to give the cost of living index not only in percentages but also-in fact preferably-in dollars and cents. Averages are deceptive and percentages are deceptive; but people understand dollars and cents. I quote as a good example the Labour Gazette, which publishes wage statistics from time to time. When those statistics are given, they are given in both ways, both in percentages, in terms of an index figure, and in actual dollars and cents. I think that information as to the cost of living furnished by the bureau to our people in terms of dollars and cents would be much more useful than it is at the present time merely in terms of a rather unreal index figure. I realize that if it were in dollars and cents, which would make it a little bit more understandable to our people, it might at times be more useful or more embarrassing, depending upon from which side of the house the figures are used. But that really does not matter. The purpose of getting statistics is to be able to use the knowledge we have about life in this country in order to improve it in every possible way.
One speaks as a layman when he talks about these things and realizes that the scientific people who are engaged in this business may have comments to make one way or the other. But I am sure it would improve the usefulness of the information the bureau give us about the cost of living if they were to do these two things: first of all, bring it up to date in terms of 1948 standards, or, shall I say, 1948 ideals as to our standard of living; and, second, find some way of giving the country a cost of living index not only in terms of percentages, but also in terms of dollars and cents. I just wished to make those suggestions, but at the

same time I desired to join with others in saying that we are indeed grateful for the work that is done and the service that is rendered to this country by the dominion bureau of statistics.
Mr. GORDON B. ISNOR (Halifax): I wish to deal with the general principle of this bill, Mr. Speaker; but first I want to join with those who have already paid tribute to the valuable work being done by the officials of the dominion bureau of statistics. As a businessman, more than once I have felt a little bit sore and vexed to think I had to fill out certain forms, particularly during the busy war period. But the more often I filled out those forms, and in turn received information from the bureau, the greater was my appreciation of the real value of my figures to them and of their figures to me. It was enlightening to me to be able to follow the trend of business in other sections of the country, to make a comparison of my business with those in other centres, and to follow the general trend of the various lines. I believe we should be very grateful that as head of this department we have a man with the ability of Mr. Marshall.
I am not going to deal with any particular sections; but, as I understand it, the general principle of this bill is to provide for the gathering of information which will be helpful to all parts of the country; the organizing of a system of co-ordinated social and economic statistics pertaining to the whole of Canada and to each of the provinces therof, and so on. That is the general principle. You can break it down into figures giving information with respect to certain things, such as the cost of living, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles); figures relating to trends, as well as the census and other duties enumerated and outlined in section 32. I am dealing with the information the bureau will give us to indicate the economic condition of one section of the country in comparison with that of the others.
Just to explain my position, generally we look upon Canada as divided into five sections. You could take the maritime provinces as one section, Quebec as the next, then Ontario, then the three prairie provinces and finally British Columbia. If you were to analyse those five sections I believe you would find a great centralization, not only of population but of industry, in the two provinces of Ontario and Quebec. If you look back to confederation and study the reason for the maritimes joining, remembering that it was for the purpose of developing trade in the maritime provinces and of assisting the other

Statistics Act
provinces, you will find that, instead of assisting us, it has not only pushed the population into the central portion of our country but developed that portion far beyond what may have been thought possible by those residing in Ontario and Quebec at that ime. To a very great extent our wealth is centred in those provinces. Look at the population. Of the 11,506,655 people in Canada, some 33 per vent are in Ontario and 29 per cent in Quebec, or a total of 62 per cent of our population in those two provinces. Then, if we look at the income we find that the income of those provinces far exceeds that of any other section of Canada. And because of the hon. gentleman's suggestion, I am going to offer one of my own with respect to greater consideration for the maritimes and other parts of Canada, other than Quebec and Ontario.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Hazen) and his reference to the report of the royal commission on maritime claims, which consisted of Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, the late Hon. subtopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was discussing the general principle underlying Bill No. 326, respecting the dominion bureau of statistics. I would refer first to the reference made by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Hazen) to the recommendations of Sir Andrew Duncan as they are set forth in the report of the royal commission on maritime claims at page 44. paragraph 39. Sir Andrew emphasized the lack of certain statistics relating to trade between the provinces, and strongly urged that these difficulties should be overcome, so that on this phase of internal trade statistics could be made regularly available at as early a day as possible.
I support that thought and I urge that the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and of his parliamentary assistant be directed to that recommendation, so that they might embody a section in the bill or, if that is not feasible, so that they might suggest to the bureau of statistics that an effort be made to compile that information. I believe it would be a real help to us in interprovincial trade relations, one which does not exist at the present time.
I have pointed out the great centralization of trade in Ontario and Quebec. While I am prepared to give credit to those provinces for the splendid manner in which they have built up their trade, I say it is not a healthy sign from a dominion-wide standpoint. And it is with that in mind that I make the suggestion which I am now about to make, and which I had intended to discuss when I took part in this debate. What I am about to discuss is centred around the same spirit as I believe existed in the United States when that country dealt with the Geneva trade agreements. Acting in a generous manner, they did not think only of themselves, but rather of the good they could do to the weaker and smaller nations throughout the world. And I believe they had particular reference to Canada, too. We gain by the Geneva agreements, and the world at large will enjoy more friendly relationships, from the standpoint of trade. I believe it will do much good throughout the world in future years, apart altogether from the financial benefits.
I suggest to the minister that if that same spirit were shown by the two large industrial provinces in Canada, Ontario and Quebec, conditions throughout the country would be better. In my view a survey could be made by the Department of Trade and Commerce. I am not suggesting that a royal commission
Statistics Act

be appointed; rather I am suggesting that a survey be made which would help develop trade not only in those two central provinces, but throughout the dominion as a whole, and that it would be to our advantage as a nation to do so. Because of the terms upon which the maritime provinces and other parts of Canada entered confederation; because of the benefits we expected from confederation, and because of the grounds upon which the dominion has granted special aids to the provinces,
I am suggesting that the minister should authorize an investigation as to the possibilities of similar trade arrangements among the various provinces, and particularly the development of trade between the industrial centres of Ontario and Quebec and the other sections of Canada, with a view to selling goods-this is the important part of my suggestion, and I am sticking closely to the principle of the bill-manufactured in Ontario and Quebec to the people in other provinces at the same laid-down cost as those goods are supplied to buyers in the two central provinces.
If we had such a survey I believe it would be shown that goods could be sold to all sections of Canada at the same laid-down price. It would not be a great trade hindrance, so far as the further development of industrial centres in Ontario and Quebec is concerned. On the contrary, it would create additional possibilities and perhaps give other sections of Canada which are not so fortunate as the two large industrial provinces a greater opportunity to enjoy to a certain extent the prosperity to which all people in Canada are entitled.
I could go on and say that Canada is a wonderful country, and make other statements of that kind, but possibly I would be called to order if I did.
Before taking my seat, I should like to make reference to the publications of the bureau of statistics. I believe they have done an exceptionally fine job in their latest publication, which deals with the maritime provinces in their relation to the national economy of Canada. This issue just reached my desk within the last few days, and I have not had an opportunity to do more than to give it casual perusal. It contains information, however, which is of real value to every Canadian who is interested in the welfare of his country. I believe it should be made available to every library in Canada and should be used as a book of reference by every member of parliament who is anxious to see, not a limited picture, but rather the whole picture of Canada.
This afternoon the "Canadian Statistical Review" for April reached my desk. That, too, is a valuable publication. With sufficient
information of this kind, I believe we could develop the budget I have in mind, that of placing the facts before the whole country so as to create a greater interest in sections outside Ontario and Quebec.
Perhaps I have said all I require to say at this time. In closing, I should like to make one further reference to the maritime provinces. Out of a total population in Canada of about 11,500,000, we find that in the maritime provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island there are only
1,100,000.	We occupy only a small place, perhaps, in the eyes of certain sections of Canada. But we are still part of this dominion. As such we should be entitled to enjoy the prosperity which is so evident in the two central industrial provinces. Within a radius of a hundred miles of Toronto we find a third of the population of the dominion. This density of population makes that area an important one, and gives it an advantage which those of us in the far-flung sections do not enjoy.
Although we are a small part of the dominion, we have sent men to fill every important position Canada has to offer. In the past we have sent important men to the House of Commons; men like Sir Charles Tupper, Sir Robert Borden, Viscount Bennett, W. S. Fielding, Edgar Rhodes, and J. L. Ralston who passed away recently. In addition to all these is our present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley). I am reminded of a question which was asked of an outstanding Halifax citizen when visiting New York about a week ago. The New Yorker said, "Tell me about this institution of yours, Dalhousie University. Is it a large place?" The reply was, "It is not as large as many of your educational institutions, but it does occupy an important place in the life of Canada, and it stood out particularly during the war years." He went on to say that Canada's war effort had centred around five or six key positions: the finance department, because it was necessary to have money to carry on the war; the department of munitions; the research council; the three branches of the defence department, army, navy and air force; and then he made this significant statement: "In the finance department we had Colonel Ralston, then we had the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, as Minister of Finance during the war period, both of them connected with Dalhousie University. In the Department of Munitions and Supply we had another man closely connected with Dalhousie University, one who had taken a very important part in its life, the

Statistics Act
Right Hon. C. D. Howe. At the head of the research council we had Doctor C. J. Mackenzie. At the head of the army we first had the late Norman Rogers; then we had Colonel Ralston, and at the head of the navy we had the Hon. Angus Macdonald. Mr. HAROLD W. TIMMINS (Parkdale): Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary assistant, when introducing this bill respecting the dominion bureau of statistics, said that the bureau and the bill itself were intended to cover all the important statistical fields of government. In addition to having the thing revised and brought up to date, I suggest that the cost of living index should be compiled on a regional basis, because the cost of living in some parts of the country, in comparison with other parts, is away out of line. I know that in the part of the country from which I come we have the highest cost of living in Canada. That is understandable when one takes into consideration the matter of freight rates, and so forth. The cost of living index should be compiled on a regional basis, instead of a certain number of cities in Canada and a certain number of items being taken and an arbitrary figure being set which certainly does not reflect the actual cost of living as it obtains in different sections of the country.

I, too, want to compliment the dominion bureau of statistics on the recent survey of the maritime provinces. I have gone through this survey and marked it pretty well. I have read every word of it. It certainly sets out the disabilities of the maritimes, but the sad part of statistics is that all they do is to set out the disabilities. They recommend nothing. The bureau of statistics has done an excellent job over the years. It has compiled many reports similar to this one, but unfortunately they go to the archives to gather dust, and nothing is ever done about them. This last one on the maritimes is very revealing. It shows the inequality that exists in the distribution of the national income as between the maritimes and the rest of Canada. I am going to read an editorial from the Halifax Herald, which compliments the bureau of statistics on the compilation of this last survey of the maritimes in relation to the national income of Canada. This short editorial compliments those who drafted the report, and tells the story better than I could do it. I am going to conclude with this. The editorial reads:
The bureau of statistics has shown, in a study, that Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces are less prosperous than the rest of Canada. But the cold figures of the study can never emphasize the gravity of the situation so strikingly as the news that 200 children in Halifax lack shoes.
That is the meat of the matter. We compile statistics and show the inequalities which exist as between province and province-we have been doing that for at least thirty years-yet nothing has ever been done to try to remedy the situation or cure the disabilities that the cold, hard statistics set out. The fact of the matter is that the trend is in reverse. The answer is not statistics. So far as the maritimes are concerned, we have all kinds of statistical proof as to what is needed. The problem in the maritimes is financial; it is an economic problem. Right at the present time small industries in Nova Scotia are not able to secure capital to expand their plants, despite the fact that the statistical report proves that a lot of subsidiary industry is needed in that end of the country. This survey shows it clearly.
Recently I met in this city people who required a few thousand dollars to expand plants that are already in operation, and they could not get the money. The banks will not give it to them. They have no redress from the Industrial Development bank, which I thought was designed to create small industry, complementary to the major set-ups. The-

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the bill. I wish to express my appreciation of the work done by the officials and ithe employees of the bureau of statistics. I think it is a work that is not fully appreciated by a large number of the Canadian people because of their lack of knowledge and understanding of its importance and extent. These officials and employees carry on, as it were, behind the scenes, without fanfare or publicity, and I am pleased to see that this bill provides for the development and extension of what I consider to be one of the most important services of government.
I wish also to express my support of some suggestions put forward this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I will not repeat them, but I thought they were sound, and the government should give them every consideration.
I also wish to commend the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) and the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Richard) on their observations concerning interprovincial trade statistics, which are most necessary. I trust that the government will give that point consideration.
During the recent sittings of the veterans affairs committee many members of that committee were, I know, much impressed with the factual way in which evidence on the cost of living was presented. The people who are gathering statistics and correctly analysing them and interpreting them according to certain principles require long and special training, and that type of person is not generally recognized because there is no publicity, nothing spectacular about the work. In my opinion a great number of the improvements which we hope to bring about in the way of social reforms, economic organization, the development of our natural resources, transportation and so on will be brought about as a result of the basing of our conclusions upon figures and statistics provided by the bureau of statistics; that is, on facts.
One other suggestion I might make as to the collection of statistics. It would be inter-

Statistics Act
esting for the western and the maritime provinces to have statistics regarding the flow of profits from the flanks of Canada to Toronto and Montreal, and information concerning insurance companies which collect moneys from east and west and re-lend them to the maritimes and the western provinces for capital investment in housing, the development of farms, and business, and as a result pyramid interest receipts. The truer picture we get of the Canadian economy because of an accurate knowledge of the facts, the better are we able to judge any situation.
I am greatly impressed by the fact-and this has been the case for a long time prior to this bill coming before the house-that the Canadian people as a whole are exceedingly under-informed about the functions of the bureau of statistics and the information that can be obtained. While technically I believe it is correct to say anyone can obtain that information, I am quite sure that generally throughout the country the great majority of the people are not aware of the mine of information obtainable from the bureau of statistics. I believe the government should carry on some publicity campaign in that respect.
This evening we have had mentioned a report which, as I understand it, deals purely with the maritimes and which quotes figures in connection with a certain situation there. From that report people are able to draw conclusions and on it are able to base opinions for improving the situation which the figures in that report indicate. I think the government should do something to see that representative organizations throughout this country are well informed on the activities of the bureau of statistics and on the information which can be obtained from that source. I would suggest that adult organizations throughout this country should be seriously concerned in playing their part to bring this information to the attention of a greater number of Canadians. The strength of democracy rests on understanding and knowledge of facts. The more we have of those attributes throughout this country the stronger will our democracy be.
I think also that more information in this connection could be brought to the attention of the school children. I have been the chairman of a school board for some years, and have been dissatisfied at the condition which existed, and the same condition exists today to some extent. It seems that those who prepare the textbooks and arithmetic courses are inclined to be over-academic and to be divorced from the practical stream of events, or shall I say, from the facts of life.
Let us take as an example our books on arithmetic or mathematics. Very often they are designed to have the pupils solve certain questions on certain subjects which are not related to the daily life of those children or their parents or to the economic activities in the district in which they live. I believe that something should be done to remedy that situation. The bureau of statistics could provide a great fund of information for the development of sound practical textbooks on arithmetic and mathematics in this country, so that the boys and girls going through our schools, in learning the processes of arithmetic and mathematics, would also come to understand the economic arrangements in our country, the situation as it exists with regard to production, population and so on. In my opinion this is a great field for the findings of the bureau of statistics to be used and introduced more fully into our educational system.
The national film board could well develop a series of pictures outlining the functions of government. While in our schools, cursory teaching is given on the British North America Act, the dominion parliament, the provincial legislatures and so on, there is little information on the function of government as it is related to the departments of government. I believe that the more we can get our older people and our children to understand how the government functions in this country-for instance, to understand what the Department of National Health and Welfare is, and its functions, what the bureau of statistics stands for and what it is-the sounder will be our democracy. I believe that the more we are able to create among the people a fuller understanding of the functions of government, the better will they be able to form judgments and sound opinions concerning any situation.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I again suggest, and bring to the attention of hon. members as a whole, that I have thought for a long time that the records, figures and findings of the bureau of statistics would make an excellent basis for the publication of books on arithmetic and mathematics more closely allied to the life which our children will have to live when they reach adult age.

There is one problem in connection with the publications generally; that is, that great numbers of inquiries are received as to the possibility of having statistics provided on subjects other than those at present covered. Another point emphasized by hon. members on all sides of the house had to do with the question of interprovincial trade. That point comes specifically under section 32; and of course most of the discussion was based on a paragraph contained in the report of the royal commission on maritime claims, the so-called Duncan report. Since that time, there has been a great development in the field of internal trade statistics. For instance, in 1931 the first census of retail, wholesale and service establishments was taken. The bureau now issues monthly and annual data pertaining to some of these establishments.

However, in the field of interprovineial trade, as opposed to internal trade generally, there are some serious difficulties, and I should like to take a moment specifically to point out some of them to hon. members. First, there is the development of motor transport in the transportation of goods. Statistics concerning this type of traffic would have to be included, but with the present practices of the motor transport industry many of the firms do not keep records in sufficient detail to be of use in interprovineial trade statistics. That is one difficulty. Another is that the detail now shown in the monthly traffic reports of railways would have to be considerably increased. Another is that, even if it were practicable to obtain all the data that would be essential, the cost W'ould be high. It is estimated that it would take between $300,000 and $400,000 a year. This relates only to the work of the bureau, and does not have anything to do with the added costs to the transportation and other firms supplying the data.
There is a further difficulty. Even if the complete figures on interprovineial trade were available, it would be difficult to determine their significance. Supposing province A should be shown as the source of a volume of goods for province B. Province A might * have imported many of the materials used from the United States, or from some other province, so that, before the interprovineial statistics could be made up, the proper significance of that factor would have to be determined. It means that in reality province A would be only in part the source of the goods for province B; and after an attempt to unravel that complexity as between the provinces and the foreign trade, it is almost impossible to see just how the information could be obtained.
There is a further difficulty, that would cast some doubt on the real value of statistics on interprovineial trade. That is, the commodity trade by itself is only one aspect of interprovincial trade. There are the invisible items such as, for instance, the movement of tourists. How could one get the data on the movement of tourists and travelers from one province to another?

I should like to add a few remarks to the suggestion of compiling statistics respecting interprovincial trade. Such information would be most interesting. The bureau of statistics is an able body, and if it could find any way of getting that information it would be useful and interesting. The difficulties, however, I believe are almost insurm ount abl e.
I have in mind manufacturers of heavj-goods. Not only are the goods heavy, but they are invoiced at large sums of money. Some of those companies may have only ten or fifteen accounts in the whole of Canada. They- deal through large wholesale houses in the large centres of the dominion-Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver and perhaps some other centres. I know of one big firm with which I was closely associated which had only seven accounts in all Canada. The people to whom they shipped trainloads of material, in turn shipped it throughout Canada. So that the large manufacturing institution in Toronto might ship ten carloads of boilers or radiators to a jobber in Montreal who, in turn, might ship it to the maritime provinces or back to eastern Ontario, northern Ontario or Manitoba.
It looks to me like a difficult procedure, if the bureau would hope to have any accurate information on the subject. If it were available, however, it would be interesting to have.
I do not believe it would disclose what my hon. friend to my left has suggested, that interprovincial trade is a one-way street; not

by any means. We want to develop it, so that when a carload of one class of goods is shipped to the east a carload of another class will be shipped back. That is real trade; and if the bureau of statistics can produce any information along those lines it would be both interesting and helpful.

subtopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS
speechtext: Does the parliamentary assistant to the minister think the basis of dollar value is of any use without an accompanying table of the quantities of the things produced? What I have in mind is this. We find that the dollar value of our trade in a certain commodity is so much. It may be that we are manufacturing only fifty per cent of what we used to manufacture; yet the dollar value remains the same. I want to get the opinion of the statistics department as to what use dollar value is without accompanying production figures of the article being dealt with.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS
speechtext: I think the answer to that is this. With some items there is no measuring value other than the dollar value. But there is this difficulty, that certain statistics which are very useful include items that cannot be measured in other than dollar value.

subtopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS
speechtext: Agreed, but the point I am trying to make, and I want you to agree with me, is this. In other words, they can have no meaning unless we have one column showing the dollar value, and another column showing the production figures. Is that not an accurate statement?

I want to thank the parliamentary assistant for the comments he made some time ago on my suggestions with regard to the cost of living index. I was indeed pleased to note his favourable reply to the effect that the bureau is at present working on a new base or norm for this important index.
However I should like to say a few additional words with reference to my other suggestion, namely, that an attempt be made to give the public an index in terms of dollars and cents. I was glad to note his statement that the statutory authority for the bureau to do this is already provided, so that what I am really doing is making a suggestion through him to the officials of the bureau.
The parliamentary assistant said this would be difficult. I believe he said that one would have to find some average, and that the dollar and cents figure which would be given would therefore in a sense be unreal. I agree that all averages are unreal except for one fictional person, the so-called famous average man, and they are also deceptive. But I point out that that is even more true of the index figure the way it is now given. My contention is that if this could be translated into dollars 5849-3034
and cents it would be much more readily understood by the people of the country.
At the present moment I believe the cost of living index stands at 152. What that means is that today it costs 152 per cent of what it cost during the period from 1935 to 1939 to buy a certain arbitrary quantity of goods and services. That arbitrary quantity was the amount that could be bought for $1,453.80,
broken down as follows:
Food	 $443.00
Shelter	 209.50
Fuel and light	 90.50
Clothing	 165.80
Home furnishings	 125.70
Miscellaneous (health, personal care, transportation, recreation, life insurance)	 319.40
Other items	 39.90
These were the items included in the index, and the quantities that could be purchased by these amounts were considered as the norm in the period 1935 to 1939. The total added up to $1,453.80. When we say today the cost of living index stands at 152 it simply means that to go into the market and buy the same quantity of goods that was bought for that figure in the previous period would now cost 152 per cent of that figure, or $2,209.77.
Let me bring both of these figures down to monthly and weekly figures. They would mean, in other words, that what it cost S121 a month to buy in 1935-39 now costs $183.92 a month; or again that what it cost $27.96 a week to buy in 1936 to 1939 now costs $42.49 a week. I have given the figures for the three periods, the year, the month and the week. Let me now stick with the figure for the week. What this all adds up to, as I see it, is this. When the dominion bureau of statistics tells us that the cost of living index is 152 it is simply saying that it cost $27.96 a week to buy a certain quantity of food and services in 1935 to 1939 for a certain group of Canadian families, and it now costs $42.49.
If the bureau were to say that the cost of living stands at $42.49 there would, of course, still be something unreal about that, in that it would be only the experience of the average man, who does not exist, and it would be only in terms of that arbitrary allotment or assortment of goods and services chosen by the bureau in 1935-39. That is true, but at least I contend it would give a better idea to the Canadian people as to where the cost of living really stands. My hope is that, when the bureau works out a new base or norm, it will arrive at that base or norm after consulting experts in the field of nutrition and health, and that it will tell us what the figure is for a decent, respectable Canadian living standard and give us that in dollars
Statistics Act

and cents. And then from here on, let us be told what the cost of that decent Canadian living standard amounts to in dollars and cents and whether it goes up or comes down.
I am not a statistician and I may be getting beyond my depth. I admit that candidly, but it seems to me that this is common sense and that if we could move in this direction the cost of living figure would be more understandable to the Canadian people generally and it would be more useful to all of us in trying to arrive at policies whereby something could be done about the cost of living and the standard of living of our people.
However, for the moment I wish to thank the parliamentary assistant for the assurance that the bureau is working on the matter.

All our maritime men have spoken on this bill that is before us, and I thought I might join in the discussion either to support what they have said or to agree in part or to disagree as the case might be. The hon. senior member for Halifax stated, with reference to the population of the maritimes, that it was 1,100,000. Well, our province of Prince Edward Island is part of the 100,000 and not of the 1,000,000.
The bureau of statistics is one of the great things in this country, either from the provincial point of view or from the point of view of the country as a whole. The gathering of statistics is important, and if they were analysed properly the result would be to extricate governments from many of the difficulties they get into. All we have to do is to look at the transportation question which we discussed some time ago and the increase that was involved.
In section 32 there is little reference to transportation and different systems of transportation, the long haul of freight and the short haul. No government or commission, if these statistics had been available to it, would have come to the conclusion that there should be a universal increase in freights all over the country.
While we may be gathering statistics, we are not having them analysed for the benefit of the people. This is exemplified in connection with the long haul of freight. The government may have had the statistics, and no doubt the Canadian National Railways had them for the last month with reference to the freight on the long haul originating in Prince Edward Island. During the month of April, which is the only one for which I have been able to get statistics, 2,600 cars of freight inward and outward were moving on the long haul. Of these, more than 1,800 were outward and 760 were inward, all going to the

benefit of the long haul freight rate. If we in our province had had those statistics, with a proper analysis of them, I do not believe that we would have been subjected to a twenty-one per cent increase in our freight rates.
In this section, 32, there is very little with regard to the collecting of statistics on transportation, which, after all, is the most important factor in the economic welfare of any province.
I am glad that the hon. senior member for Halifax has become a convert to the stamp freight idea, about which I have spoken three or four times. I notice he is now in favour of the idea that goods originating in Ontario and in Montreal should be sold at the same rate to the retailer, no matter where the retailer lives. I am glad, as I say, that he has been converted.

I wish to call the attention of the minister for four or five minutes to certain matters in connection with which I have had a good deal of correspondence with him. There is a large surplus in the department at the present time, and I am asking for better working conditions and hours of labour for some of the rank and file of the post office. In our city we have recently taken over one of the buildings used during the war, situated at the foot of Bay street, where the army had its storehouse, and the navy and other branches were accommodated. I refer to the mail order department. The surpluses for the past six years have been: 1941, $1,683,000. That was a war year. In 1942 it was $4,492,000; in 1943, $4,126,000; in 1944, $12,585,000; in 1945, $11,442,000; in 1946, $10,905,913; in 1947, last year, $8,773,574. So far so good. I notice that our city has a postal revenue of over $15 million; I think it is about $15,250,000. I believe that Montreal has a revenue of only about $10,100,000. I have the figures here. In that connection I may say there are far more substations in

Supply-Post Office
Montreal than there are in Toronto, although the revenue is nearly $5 million less. I think the time has come when some of these profits should be used to reduce the postal rates.
The post office is a magnificent public utility. It has the endorsement of all the people of our city and, I think, of practically all the people in the whole country. It is a well-conducted public utility. I believe the time has come when there should be some additional reduction in the postal rates which were largely raised shortly before the war and during the war when so many of our men and women were in the forces. The time has now come for better working conditions. I should think in the city we should have a one-cent drop letter rate, and for the rest of the country a three-cent rate. If that were done, it would mean that there would be some reduction of the surplus.
I think the time has come when, in our city and throughout Canada, the minister should own, occupy and manage his own public building. I do not think it is fair to have the Department of Public Works over the present minister, who has a vast experience in business as a lawyer. I think it would be far better if control were transferred from the Department of Public Works to the Post Office Department. I would make that suggestion.
The other suggestion I wish to make is that we should have a more progressive public utility. It is progressive. Valuable services are being given at low cost, and some improvements are being made, I will admit, in labouring conditions, with regard to holidays at week ends and at Christmas time and matters like that. But I think the time has come when the post office should branch out and assume some of the functions performed by the British post office, because our post office has not improved greatly in functions up to 1948.
I do not wish to delay the minister in getting his estimates through, but I hope there will be some reform along the lines I have suggested. The minister should have full jurisdiction over the ownership of the building, repairs and all that kind of thing. A number of old buildings have been used, and they might be put to other uses. Some public buildings and post offices are built where the revenues received are not commensurate with their size. For example, in some of the cities and towns large public buildings are being built where one about half the size would be commensurate with the business done. I believe that should be a good principle to follow, because the cost of building today is
almost prohibitive. It is now about three times what it used to be. I believe it would be far better if a cheaper form of building were provided, with more windows and all that kind of thing. A more modern structure could be built. I think the revenue should be considered. If a public building is to be built in town A, B, or C, consideration should be given to what the revenue of that public building will be in town A, B, or C. There should be some relationship between the size of the building and the use to which it is to be put, its functions, and how many departments are using it. I think the time has come when we should have some reduction in rates which apply to the post office department of our city, and not have the surplus used outside for other purposes.

I just wish to add a little to what has been said by the hon. member for Broadview and to ask a few questions. Is the minister able to give the committee the approximate number of postmen employed throughout the whole country, and the approximate number in the principal cities such as Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, and Vancouver?

In connection with what the previous
speaker said, in Toronto there are large stores like Eaton's and Simpson's, which use the mails extensively. This in large part accounts for the increase in revenue or for the larger amount of postage stamps sold in Toronto as compared with Montreal.

As to the transfer of the building of post offices to the Postmaster General, I have no objection at all as long as I am Postmaster General. If I changed my position, I might not be in favour of the change.
