The last time these
estimates were dealt with I brought up the question of more comfortable quarters in the average branch post offices in Toronto. I am aware that some, such as the West Toronto post office, are splendid, and the department deserves praise for putting up a fine branch like that. But there are other offices with quite a number of postmen, perhaps forty, more or less, much of whose work is done down in the basement of the building they happen to be in, which probably was formerly a store. In the summer those quarters are not very comfortable; it gets very hot down there.
I should like to see the department try to bring about a uniform standard of comfort for the postmen throughout the city. That may be hard to do, but I hope some way will be found of doing it. We have a wonderful civil service in Canada, and of the whole service no part does a better job than the ordinary postman. No part of the service works harder than they do, though I am not finding fault with the other departments in that regard. The difference is that the postman is out in all sorts of weather, hot or raining or snowing, usually carrying a heavy load. So when he returns to his station he is entitled to a comfortable place to rest a while before starting for home. Very few of the branch post offices have such a convenience. They may have benches to sit on, but there is not much in the way of comfort or any amenities. I should like to see that situation improved.
On the last occasion I believe I brought up the question of the remuneration of the postmen, and I understand that has been attended to, that they are now getting better remuneration. But I understand that the foreman in the office; I forget what he is called-
The supervisor.
-the man who allocates and supervises the beats, and so on, who has a responsible job, was not advanced on the last occasion. Has he been advanced since then?
Yes, everyone has been advanced to the same extent as the other employees.

I am glad to learn that; I know the minister is doing the best job he can. I think that pretty well covers the questions I wanted to ask. Personally I am proud of the whole postal service, particularly of the fine type of men employed, practically all of wThom are returned soldiers. It is seldom one hears of any malfeasance or theft or robbery, though they handle precious and valuable mail. To my mind the ordinary postman represents one class of civil servants who deserve unstinted credit.

One of the finest in Canada. This post office was built a good many years ago. Now, with the increased revenue the space has become too small for the increased work that has to be done. It is not only the work in connection with the town itself; there are ten rural mail routes running out of that post office. I would request the minister to make a survey, and if he can see his way clear to do so I would urge him to recommend to the Department of Public Works that a new post office be built in the town of Picton. If that is impossible I would suggest that at least the present building be considerably modernized.
While I am on my feet I should like to bring another matter to the attention of the Postmaster General. I refer to the employees in the post offices both in Picton and in Napanee, which town also I have the honour to represent. Those post offices are in a category which I believe includes very few others. The only member of the staff coming under the civil service is the postmaster himself. The remainder of the staff are placed there on a patronage basis, or some other basis. I am not complaining about that at all, but I say to the Postmaster General that these young men. most of whom are veterans, are not receiving wages that are nearly adequate for the work they have to do. As a matter of fact, in view of the present cost of living I do not know how they keen a home together and live.

I think that is something which should be considered at an early day. I am aware that some small consideration has been given them; but in my opinion if one man in a post office is under the civil service and eligible for superannuation and other benefits, all employees in that post office should be treated in the same way. I would urge the minister to consider seeing to it that all the employees in these post offices are brought within the civil service and given the same rights as are employed by those in other offices.

First I should like to thank the department, through the minister, for instituting a postal delivery service in the fine little town of Dundas several months ago. In connection with the philatelic division, or whatever it is called, I should like to say a word on the issue of the Princess Elizabeth stamps. I have a letter which I have preserved for this purpose, and I quote from it:
[DOT]lust a note to say many thanks for the first day cover of the Princess Elizabeth stamp that I have received from you in Ottawa. I did get a couple of other covers but yours is the only one that is hand stamped'-
I may say it was hand stamped here in the House of Commons.
-which makes it more attractive. Ottawa ran all the covers through a cancelling machine with a worn slug in it and really made a mess of all the stamps.
I merely draw this to the attention of the department in a kindly way, as the Minister of Labour would say, so that when they send out first covers on another occasion and have them stamped in Ottawa they might bear this in mind and not have some old slug doing the job.
I received a letter from the hon. gentleman in this connection, and we have advised our employees to see that this does not happen again.

Some of the post offices in the rural districts of my riding are being closed, where there may be a mail route which will serve the people. Just last week representations were made to me in connection with another post office, which is some twelve miles out. These people do not want to lose their post office, because on the rural routes they have to wait outside if they want to get a postal note. We have a great deal of snow in our part of the country, and it is very cold waiting around for the mailman. I saw the department this week about this matter, and they told me nothing would be done, but I wonder if it could not be re-
Supply-Post Office
considered. This post office is about twelve miles from my home town and about twenty miles from the next town in the other direction. They would like very much to keep their post offices.
Then, I should like to join with the previous speaker in asking that these returned men employed by the Post Office Department be put under the civil service. If a returned boy works for the post office and is receiving only 51,200, $1,500 or something like that, he should be under the civil service. The postmaster is under the new system, but I should like to see the clerks in post offices placed in the same position as postmasters.

I wish to make my annual plea to the Postmaster General for better post office buildings in the constituency of Selkirk. We have one or two good post offices there, but many of the buildings are not satisfactory.
I am pleased to see the genial Minister of Public Works in his seat, because I am sure the Postmaster General will be telling me to see him.
I have had many representations from towns in my constituency which are growing by leaps and bounds. When one sees a post office in an old broken down building it gives the whole department a bad name. I do not want to get in wrong with any other ministers, but I believe the post office is one of the best departments we have, so far as giving service to the community is concerned. To do a proper job they should have good buildings- and I would ask the Minister of Public Works to listen to what I am saying.
We have the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in many of our districts in the west. They have to have barracks and offices. It would be worth while to see one government building housing the post office and the mounted police. I do not know whether the minister has been to the town of Arborg, but if he has he will know it is a growing town. They have built a hospital for themselves, but the post office is a disgrace to the community.
What I have suggested is something which should be done. We should have better post offices for people to work in, buildings which would be a credit to the towns and the department. I have mentioned only one town; I could give the names of a dozen of them.

I have three or four matters I should like to take up .with the Postmaster General. The first is the question raised by the announcement made in the press, and I believe also in the house, to the effect that rural postmasters, or postmasters of small offices, were to be made civil servants. So far
Supply-Post Office

as I know, the necessary legislation has not gone through the house. Is it intended to introduce a bill this year, or is that to be done by order in council?

According to the rules, that is done by the Postmaster General himself. An explanation as to why it is done in that way would take some time, but I would point out that it has always been within the jurisdiction of the Postmaster General.
It is true, as the hon. member says, that a greater amount of post office revenue and a greater number of postmasters are being brought under the civil service, with fair salaries. In the meantime, in respect of post offices with revenue of over $3,000, we are now taking care of rentals ourselves to ensure that we have better places in which to install our post offices. Also, if help is required we see that the salaries of the helpers are fixed by and paid for by the department. The postmaster will have a fixed salary. Postmasters in post offices with revenue of more than $3,000 will, we hope, be eligible for superannuation, if they are not too old. In this way they become permanent employees.
We are working on this matter. A beginning has been made and we hope to be able to continue. It will be remembered, of course, that there are over 12,000 post offices in Canada, and it will take considerable time before we can establish this procedure at every point.

I thank the Postmaster
General for his answer. Is it correct to say that the proposal to make postmasters civil servants applies only to those offices with revenues at the present time over $3,000 a year?
That is right. We cannot do it for very small post offices with revenues of only $300 or $400 a year.
Was there a separate proposal, or is it part of the same proposal, to allow rural postmasters to contribute to and to come under the superannuation scheme?
It is just an experiment. We hope to do something for those who receive over $3,000. But of course we have to submit our plan first to treasury board.

I was consulted some time ago with respect to a proposal concerning which I did not know the details and upon which, for that reason, I could not give

advice. The person who consulted me said he understood if he had been there a certain number of years, made a request and made certain contributions, he might come under the superannuation scheme, even though he would not be classed as a civil servant. Is that a separate scheme, or was he misinformed?

No specific decision has yet been made on that point. We know what we would like to do, but no specific decision has been made. I should not like to say anything until it has been decided upon by the proper officers.
May we expect in the near future to have a complete statement from the Postmaster General covering both schemes?
I think I shall be able to give it next session.
Not before then?
We hope this session is not going to last very long.

I should like to ask the minister some specific questions with regard to the mail service in my own riding. I do so because I have had correspondence with him. While I appreciate the points he has made in his replies, I have not obtained the results I had hoped to obtain. Perhaps he could outline the general provisions governing.
I should like first to refer to the mail service-to and from Blue River, British Columbia. This is a divisional point on the Canadian National Railways half way between Kamloops, British Columbia, and Edmonton, Alberta. They have a growing amount of correspondence with Edmonton, and yet they find that the mail between Blue River and Edmonton must go south to Kamloops, be transferred to the Canadian- Pacific, go east to Calgary, be transferred at Calgary, and go north to Edmonton. This is a matter of some-650 miles, instead of going north from Blue River to Edmonton, a matter of about 300 miles. The answer given by the Postmaster General is that there are no mail clerks on the Canadian National Railways train.
Then they find that the same situation applies between Blue River and Vancouver. The mail to Vancouver goes to Kamloops by the Canadian National, the only railway serving that district; then it is transferred at Kamloops to the Canadian Pacific, and transhipped to Vancouver.
In both cases I have had instances cited to me of mail taking about five days to reach Vancouver or Edmonton by these roundabout routes, whereas the train itself requires only1

Supply-Post Office
fourteen hours to Vancouver and ten hours or less to Edmonton. The answer I have from the Post Office Department is that it is cheaper to do it in that way; that is, to tranship it to the Canadian Pacific rather than send it direct on the Canadian National. I cannot understand how it would not be more expensive to tranship it, recheck the letters from the bags, and send them from one railway to another. The money they save by not having a mail clerk on the Canadian National would be more than the $3,000 which they say they are saving now by having a mail clerk on the Canadian Pacific.

We are still in correspondence about this problem, and we have not got an answer to our last inquiries, because of flood conditions in that part of the country. To be frank, I would not be able to give all the particulars here, because we have so many of these problems and cannot learn the details by heart but must have the files before us. I will take note of what the hon. gentleman has asked and will take the liberty of writing him and explaining at full length.

I am glad to hear the minister say that, because, from the correspondence we had, I was under the impression that the minister's last decision was final and that a change could not be made. I take it that the matter is still under consideration?
Yes.
I am grateful for that assurance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
So that the .minister will not think there is no support on this side of the house for the point raised by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox, and reiterated by others, I feel that the assistant postmasters particularly should be made eligible for civil service benefits. I have had considerable correspondence about this matter; I must say that the minister has been most receptive, and I w'ish to thank him for his attitude. The present status of my correspondence is that, unless the revenue at a post office is $30,000 or more, the assistant postmaster will not be eligible to qualify for civil service status; and, even where the revenue is in excess of $30,000, he cannot qualify at present, although I understand that something to that end is being undertaken. I think $30,000 is too high a figure. If an assistant postmaster is necessary he should be given the privilege of qualifying for the same civil service benefits as the postmaster. The assistant postmaster in offices of the size under discussion receives a relatively small salary and is not entitled to pension or
superannuation benefits of any kind. I should like to see the minister go as far as the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox urged, and embrace all the employees, but at the moment I am appealing for consideration for the assistant postmaster. I ask the minister if he will not consider this matter further with a view to going below the $30,000 line he has apparently drawn, so that where an assistant postmaster is necessary he may be allowed to qualify for civil service status.
Yes.

I have a copy of a letter from the board of trade of Leduc in my riding concerning the post office at Leduc. They say:
Dear Sir:
The Leduc board of trade after a thorough discussion as to the needs of a larger and better post office for the town of Leduc instructed me to write you about this matter. I realize, of course, that you are fully cognizant of the situation in our town and it would avail little my dwelling upon the needs.
However, to draw this matter to your attention for your further investigation I might mention that Leduc is a growing town due to the discoveries of oil in its vicinity. The population is growing rapidly and the old post office, which is a corner of the E & S store, has been hardly large enough in the past to accommodate Leduc and its large rural mail deliveries, let alone taking care of its booming requirements.
I earnestly appeal to you that you may take into your immediate plans the urgent needs of Leduc for better and larger postal facilities.
Thanking you for your valuable time, I am, Yours truly,
R. MacLaren,
Secretary-treasurer.
I can say from my own knowledge that this post office is entirely inadequate for the postal needs of the people of Leduc and the surrounding country. It is true that, owing to oil developments, the town is crowded and a great many new people have come into it. Most certainly they are in need of larger and better postal facilities. I understand that the minister has received a copy of this letter. Can he hold out any hope that he will take action in regard to the post office at Leduc?

I can quite understand that in a place like Leduc, because of the development that is going on there, the need for postal service is increasing rapidly. For six or seven years we have not been building any post offices because of the war and post-war conditions, but we hope to be able to catch up very soon with the time lost. I know about the situation in Leduc, and we hope to be able to do something there, if not this year, at least next year.
Supply-Post Office

From time to time I have had requests for extensions of rural mail routes in my riding. I go to the Post Office Department with these representations and receive a courteous hearing, but nothing is done about the matter. I am very glad to learn tonight that the Post Office Department is in such a healthy financial condition, because it means that one of two things must be done; either the service must be extended, or the cost of the service must be reduced. Would the minister state whether there is any intention of extending rural routes, short spurs and that sort of thing, at this time?

A question
asked about one particular place is pretty difficult to answer without our having the files before us; but I can state, as a matter of principle, that we are going to extend the rural routes in different places where they should be extended, according to the regulations of the Post Office Department. For some time we have not been making extensions, and when I recently announced the all-up service by plane, I stated at the same time that we would be ready to establish and extend more rural routes.

I want to make an appeal to the Postmaster General which has been made before, namely, that he consider reducing the postage on overseas relief parcels. I have been under the impression during the past several sessions that the major portion of that charge was for conveyance of the parcels overseas. In a recent letter from the department I was instructed that twenty-five per cent of the nominal $2.50 was charged on a regular overseas relief parcel for ocean conveyance; the rest is for transportation in Canada. I feel that the Canadian postal department could very well consider reducing that amount. If only twenty-five per cent is being used for overseas transportation then the remainder, seventy-five per cent, of the $2.50, could very well be reduced. Like one other hon. member who spoke a few moments ago, I am speaking for myself on this matter. I send parcels overseas and I want some relief. This is a matter that the Postmaster General should seriously consider, and reduce the postage on the overseas relief parcels.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I wonder whether the minister would make some further comment about letter carriers and other post office employees. I have been interested in listening to the remarks about service in rural

areas, but I should like to direct his attention for a moment to the conditions of those who work in urban areas. The minister may recall that I had some correspondence with him on behalf of employees in Winnipeg who are concerned about the inadequacy of the pay increases which they received recently, and are also concerned about the classifications of letter carriers, porters, sorters and so on.
In addition, I have before me a letter which happens to be addressed to the leader of this group. It comes from one of the associations in Vancouver, expressing the same concern principally about the salary increases that were given recently when other civil service increases were announced. This letter points out, as employees of the Post Office Department in Winnipeg have pointed out to me, that in some cases these increases, long awaited, long anticipated, amounted to only $3 a month. The suggestion is that letter carriers, for example, surely should be getting for the service that they perform more than the $1,800, which is the amount that some of them receive now; it should be $2,400.
I would appreciate it if the Postmaster General would comment on this whole question of wage conditions and classification of urban post office employees. If it means that representations have to be made to the civil service commission I hope the minister will tell us that he is making these representations just as forcefully as we make them to him.

I desire to answer the hon. gentleman's question about the letter carriers. The increase which has been given to all the employees is exactly the same, $660 a year since 1939. The reason why letter carriers have not received in the last increase as much as the postal clerks, for example, is that at a certain time a high cost of living bonus was given. The amount of high cost of living bonus which was given was larger for the lower paid employees than for the higher paid. Later on, these bonuses were merged with the salaries, and the differential that existed in 1939 between the postal clerks and the letter carriers was not the same as it was before. There is a certain differential between the postal clerks and the letter carriers which has always existed. When we gave the last increase to the employees we took into consideration the fact that at a certain time between 1939 and today the letter carriers had received, through a high cost of living bonus, more than postal clerks, and this was readjusted. The letter carriers have

Supply-Post Office
contended that the increase was not large enough; but the letters which were received were not complete, because we were accused of giving an increase of only $36 to the letter carriers, while others received, let us say, about $120, if I am not mistaken. But if we took into account all the increases since 1939 it would amount to the same, $660 for everyone of them. We put the facts as they should have been put, and the letter carriers have had to admit that it was just. The letter carriers who were in the maximum bracket received only $36, because they had received a larger bonus than the postal clerks, but the readjustment at the end was $660 for every employee.
By the way I may say it is $180 more for the employees of the post office than for the employees of other departments.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Can the Postmaster
General give the present schedule of the letter carriers, minimum, intermediate and maximum rates?

Someone took the floor from me before I had concluded what I had to say. I thought the minister was going to reply to part of what I had to say. I wish to point out to him that the revenues of our city are over $15,000,000. I want to find out what the government is going to do about giving us better facilities in the Post Office Department, a great public utility. Compare your post office, that great utility, in terminal A w7ith the following public utilities: the Bell Telephone Company, the Consumers Gas Company, the Hydro Electric, Eaton's, Simpson's and all these other places where they have modem buildings. We have made no progress since confederation. At the head of Toronto street, on Adelaide street there is an old post office, one of the first buildings erected after confederation in that part of the city. I would not call it a post office. I should like to find out what the plan is for the Toronto district, because with a $15,000,000 revenue you are spending hardly any of it there. What is the program for Toronto? We have terminals A, B, C, D, and all down through the alphabet in the city. I wish to know what they are going to do. They said that they would have at the back of the Toronto post office on Lombard street, Church street, Adelaide street and Victoria street a big public square and dominion building. It cannot be done now. I do not expect that. I do expect to have some place where they can sell postage stamps. The staff are magnificent. They work under poor labour conditions. The minister has done a great
deal to improve it. I have said that. He has given holidays, improved labour conditions, and has done things like that.
Another matter I wish to mention is the difficulty of getting postage stamps. With that large revenue, I see no reason why the practice followed in the United States, where they sell postage stamps in the railway trains, could not be followed here. You get off the train coming from Toronto to Ottawa and you cannot buy a stamp at any station. During the time that the troops were demobilized in Halifax and were taken across the country, they had a great deal of difficulty. The civilian population should not have to put up with that in times like these. You cannot buy a postage stamp on the train; you cannot buy one in any railway station in Canada.
Another thing I should like to mention is the airmail service. The average letter dropped in the mailbox goes almost as quickly as an airmail letter out of Ottawa and other places. With regard to the staff in the post office, are the returned men getting the preference in these positions? Will these men get their old positions now that they have come back? In both the first and the second world war the Post Office Department contributed a larger number of men to the service than other public utilities and corporations. These men have to make out application forms, and the wages are not what they should be. It is true they have been increased, but the men have to go to 465 Bay street, where the civil service commission has a finger in the pie, and by the time the soldier gets through running around he is tired of trying to find someone who will give him some information.
One important question I wish to bring once more to the attention of the minister is the fate of the man who happens to steal thirty cents or fifty cents from the post office. The penalty is altogether too severe. We got it reduced from a three-year term after a ten-year fight here. It used to be three years, without any discretion on the part of the magistrate. For a petty offence the employee would be sent to prison and his wife and family would suffer in consequence. I fail to see why these women and their children should suffer when the breadwinner is sent away for three years, now a year in some cases by amendments to the criminal code. I suggest that proper arrangements should be made with the provinces to take care of the prisoner in some better provincial jail, and of the sufferers, the wife and family of any man who is convicted on such a charge.

Supply-Post Office

Moreover, is it British justice to maintain a spy decoy system whereby someone keeps a watch on a man and slips a decoy into his pocket? Is that a Christian principle for our Post Office Department to adopt? I say no, emphatically. It should have been abolished long ago, and I regret to see indications of this sort of thing in our police courts. Such evidence should be ruled out.
We want a more up-to-date act. We are not back in 1867. We want a British North America Act not for the dead but for the living. The Post Office Act was, until about three years ago, almost an exact copy of that of 1868. I do not think it is at all just to sentence a man to one year imprisonment now for a minor offence and have his wife and children thrown upon the municipality. I repeat, there should be some reform in this direction, and a satisfactory arrangement should be made with the provinces as to a proper place for detention.
There are many other matters that I should like to touch upon, but I have not the time tonight to deal with them. Among these I might mention money order transactions, the line-up at the post office, the length of time it takes to get service, the Canadian parcel post and so forth. Then there is the question of the post office savings bank. That used to be an important function and, with the penny bank being abolished, I hope this particular service will be improved. I would also point out the delay in collecting airmail from the boxes. In some of the post offices there are special receptacles for airmail letters. I hope there will be an improvement in the mail boxes. There is also the question of inspection service. As far as that is concerned, the sooner we abolish the notorious system, which is worthy of Hitler, of trying to induce someone to steal a letter and then penalizing him, the better.
There is also the equipment supply branch to be considered. I suggest that we need a house-cleaning in the city of Toronto, whose contribution, as I have pointed out before, amounts to $15,000,000.
Lastly, I would urge upon the minister that everything possible be done to improve the conditions in the Post Office Department in so far as they affect the returned man. He does not get his job back from the post office, notwithstanding that a law was passed, which was enforced by the deputy minister of labour, calling upon large corporations to give returned soldiers the identical jobs they had before they joined up, or some other occupation suitable to them. That has not been carried out so far as the Post Office

Department is concerned. Promotions should also be looked into for the returned1 men. I do not think the civil service commission knows much about it. The Post Office Department is one public utility which the Canadian people support and everyone likes to see the postman making his rounds. The children like to see him. I trust, therefore, that improvements will be made in the various directions I have suggested.
The Postmaster General was about to give me a partial answer to my question regarding overseas parcels when some energetic member jumped up and prevented it. Can he give the answer now?

First, in regard to the postal clerk, the maximum is $2,400, and in the case of the letter carrier the maximum is $2,160. The letter carrier's salary of $2,124 was increased by $36 only, but this $36 makes up what the postal clerk received before.
As to parcel gifts, I might take as an example a parcel of fifteen pounds. The handling at the office of origin costs ten cents; the handling at the exchange office, five cents; land transportation in Canada, sixty cents; Atlantic sea transport, ninety cents; British cost, fifty-one cents. We may receive a parcel of that size in Vancouver and we put it on the sea transport for eighty cents. It costs ninety cents on the vessel and fifty-one cents for delivery of the parcel in Britain, where distances are never as long as they are here. We have to prepay all this, because we have to account to Britain for the fifty-one cents. Of course we have to pay the ship ninety cents.
This question came up quite often during the war and it has arisen ever since, but when we compare what we are receiving with what Britain receives, I do not think we can reduce our receipts for this service in comparison with what Britain receives for the service rendered there. It would be really another gift we would be making in addition to the gifts our citizens are sending to their friends in England, because it amounts to only a small part of our total receipts. For one pound we receive 5, 3, 5, plus 8, or 21 cents; 8 cents of the 21 cents is for transport on the ship, and Britain takes 17 cents per pound parcel. Altogether it is 38 cents. What we charge is only 21 cents, and to reduce that would be simply to make a gift, since we are charging just what it costs us without making half a cent profit.

The Postmaster Genera! mentioned a fifteen-pound parcel. I understand that the weight of gift parcels is twenty pounds.

Supply-Post Office
I took the figure "15" because that appears on. the table I have.
Were those figures which the minister gave for a twenty-pound parcel?
I have not the twenty-pound parcel figures here. My tabulation stops at fifteen.

What prompted my bringing up this matter tonight was the letter I had from the Postmaster General's office, signed by the Postmaster General himself, in which I was informed, as I stated previously, that twenty-five per cent additional of the postage is paid for the conveyance of the parcel across the Atlantic. I thought that was a small percentage of the whole, and I felt we should probably reduce it to some extent to give relief to the people who were sending parcels to relatives overseas. If the figures the Postmaster General gave me a few minutes ago are on a twenty-pound parcel, they add up- and I have added them up roughly-to $2.16, which is not $2.50.
The $2.16 applied to the fifteen pounds, and we charge only $2 for that.

I have a question or two I should like to ask, and this is about the only item I can see under which I can properly ask them. Who was responsible for imposing that nuisance tax on the people who make use of post office savings accounts? Some months ago they found themselves confronted with this nuisance tax when they make a withdrawal. I should like to know who was responsible for imposing that tax and what was the reason for it. In withdrawing money from the post office savings account, it is not a matter of issuing cheques on a bank account; because one must appear in person, make his application and withdraw the money there at the post office. He has not the privilege of issuing a cheque against the account, as can be done with a savings account or any other account with a bank. From what I can see, this is only a nuisance, and I should like to know the reason why it was imposed on the people.

The savings account branch we have in the postal service is not meant to be a bank in the usual sense in which we use the bank here in Canada. If you withdraw money from that by cheque, you pay three cents or six cents, according to the amount of your withdrawal, as you would on any other bank account.
What is the rate?
The rate is three cents, the same as at any other bank. It is three cents on anything up to $100 and six cents on anything over $100.
When was that impost put on, or has it always been there?
I am informed that this was put on a few months ago. But it is the amount that is being charged by any other bank in Canada for the withdrawal of money by cheque.

I believe it is more than a few months ago. It must be at least half a year, if not more. But what the minister says is only a partial answer to the questions I asked. In the first place, his answer shows that it is only a nuisance tax. The revenue that it brings in does not amount to anything. As to comparing withdrawing money from the post office with withdrawing money from any other institution that you have money in, you are not in the same position with the post office savings account, because with any other bank account you can issue cheques against it. I have no objection to placing my stamp on any of those cheques. But when the individual must appear in person before the wicket, make out an application for a 850 or $100 withdrawal, and then is subject to this nuisance tax, he must fish around to find three cents to pay that little tax. It is not that it brings in any revenue; and it only results in a nuisance for the post office employees when they are making out the application for withdrawal and in their accounting with regard to the moneys handled in the branch.

My plea is for the old fellows in the post office. During the war, as we know, when the soldiers were overseas the older men were brought into the post office and were told that their jobs were simply temporary, that they would have to make way for the returned men when they came back. When the returned men came back, according to my experience, they were given back their jobs, which is only proper and fair. But the old chaps, most of whom were experienced clerks in the urban centres, were kept on for a time. Then, after a while their employment came down to, we will say, four days a week. Latterly they have been getting probably three days a week. Then they have been cut down to four or five hours a day in the city. These men held the fort for us pretty well during the war days. They are mostly men over sixty years of age. They cannot find
Supply-Post Office

employment anywhere else. They are doing a good job in the post office. They are efficient.
My plea to the Postmaster General is that he direct the postmasters in the urban centres such as Toronto to do what they can to keep these men in employment. The post office is doing fairly well financially. We do not want the post office ever to make so much money that we shall have to take money away from it and use it for some other purpose. I would ask the minister that he direct the postmaster in Toronto, where we have a great many of these men-and they have been efficient clerks during the war and since-to give them something more in the way of employment.
One more thing. In Toronto we have a most disgraceful main post office. It is really just a barracks. This does not come exactly in the department of the minister. He does not construct the buildings; nevertheless, he does make recommendations. Our post office may be in the wrong place. At any rate, I worked there as a boy, when I was going to university, and that is a long while ago. It was pretty much a derelict building even in those days. I am hoping that the minister will not wait until some more Liberal members come from the city of Toronto before he gives us a new post office, because that may be a long time.
Mr. BERTRAND (Laurier); We never have those ideas in the department.
Mr. TIMMINS; No, I know the postmaster has not. But then, of course, he is only one in the cabinet. He cannot have it all his own way. I hope that this year, now that we have expanding revenues, he will tell the cabinet members, the men on the executive council, that we should like to have a new post office in Toronto, and that we should like it to be number one on the list.

I wish to bring up a matter to which I think the minister should give serious attention. Last Christmas at Maple Creek a person was engaged to assist in the Christmas rush. The postmistress there was convicted in a Saskatchewan court of paying less than the minimum wage under the laws of Saskatchewan. The matter was finally brought to the Supreme Court of Canada, and the federal government counsel argued that both employer and employee were in the postal service of Canada, under the jurisdiction of parliament, and that therefore the provincial legislation did not apply to them.
I do not intend to quarrel with the actions of the courts; it is their business to discover what the law is and to apply it. I presume the Supreme Court of Canada was correct in its

finding; and the point is that if it was correct something is radically wrong with the administration of any government department that refuses to pay an employee $18.50 a week in this day and age.
The laws of Saskatchewan were made for the benefit of the people of that province by the government duly elected; and if the federal government is not prepared to permit these people to come under the wage laws of that province, then the federal government should see to it that they are paid proper wages, in line with the minimum wages of that or any other province having minimum wage legislation. That amount is certainly not exorbitant.
As I say, I am not trying to blame the postmistress. It was up to her to get the job done, and she was not going to spend any more money than was permissible. But when the court finds that both she and the temporary employees come under the Post Office department-and that is the finding-then the federal department and the administration are responsible for seeing to it that their employees get at least the minimum wage for the work they do.

As I explained a few moments ago, we have changed the rules. In the revenue post offices today we pay the postmasters fixed salaries, which will entitle them to superannuation, and so forth. The postmaster formerly paid these employees himself, out of his revenue, and at times we found that he was not very generous with them. Since April 1, however, we have changed that procedure, and that was one reason we did so, in order to see to it that the employees are paid reasonable salaries. We also see that the post office is located according to our specifications, so that these postmasters will not gyp us, if that word may be used, in regard to the location. We are going to see that the smaller post offices are located in better quarters.	.

The amount is high enough, indeed; but if the hon. gentleman would take into consideration the fact that during the Christmas season, in Toronto, for example, we have to obtain over seven thousand temporary employees, and in Montreal around six thousand temporary employees, he would see the reason for it. In every city we require temporary employees at that time of year, some of whom may work for a month and others for shorter periods. To have all those names appear in the estimates would enlarge the book considerably; but all those expenditures are audited. It covers employees who may work for two or four or five days, while others may work for a week or more. If the hon. gentleman emphasized the point I might be able to bring in a list of these employees, but it would be a difficult return to prepare. I do not think that expenditure can be treated in any other way.

That is a satisfactory answer. Never before have we been given any idea of the extent of this temporary employment. Now the Postmaster General has given us some idea, which is quite satisfactory to me.
In all the city offices we require over 25,000 temporary employees.

How do you determine the yearly income of postmasters in small villages? Some of them, I understand from some of my constituents who work in these places, must be there all day because of the hours, and they cannot undertake other work. They tell me they can hardly live. Is there any way of putting a floor under the income of these people, or how do you determine what their living will be?
Mr. BERTRAND (Laurier); We have small offices where the revenue is below $100 a year. In those offices the postmaster has the privilege of doing something else. He is generally a restaurant keeper or a storekeeper, and he keeps the post office in his store. But even if a postmaster has a revenue of only $12 or $13 or $15 we pay him a minimum of $120. A postmaster in a very small village who also keeps a store, in which the post office occupies a small booth, receives at least $120, though the revenue may be only $25 a year.

I am thinking of the man in a place where there are three other stores, who has not the capital to open a store of his own, where there is not room for another grocery store, but who must keep his post office open all day, six days a week. Is there any way of determining what he will live on? How can he go out and work as a carpenter if he has to stay in the post office?

He must not take a job as postmaster unless that is to be simply a by-product, if I may call it, of what he is going to earn. It must be a man or woman who can keep a little post office in the house or in the store. If he is a carpenter he had better not also be the postmaster.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
What is the business for tomorrow?

speechtext: We shall go into supply of the Post Office Department, hoping that we may make a little more progress; and then trade and commerce, reconstruction and supply, justice, Secretary of State and public works.
